newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Political violence seen hurting Sri Lanka peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: Political violence seen hurting Sri Lanka peace hopes.

text.p: The upsurge of political violence over the recent killing of a ruling coalition lawmaker could weaken prospects of bipartisan consensus needed to end Sri Lanka's ethnic war, analysts and diplomats said on Tuesday.

Mob violence and attacks on members of the opposition United National Party (UNP) following Nalanda Ellawala's killing on February 11 could widen differences between UNP and the ruling People's Alliance (PA), they said.
Police said at least one man died when mobs torched shops owned by UNP supporters in the southern Ratnapura district.

Ellawala was shot dead during a roadside quarrel in the southern town of Kuruwita on the eve of the deadline for nominating candidates to the March 21 local elections, the government's first popularity test since winning power in 1994.
UNP lawmaker Susantha Punchinilame, one of the main suspects in the murcer, surrendered to a court last week after several days in hiding.
"There's no sense of constructive bipartisanship," said a Western diplomat, who declined to be identified.

"The violence is disturbing," he added. "With very high perceived stakes in the poll and emotions running high, if one party or the other does particularly well at the expense of the other, I do not see them coming together," the diplomat said.

The PA needs UNP's support in parliament to pass its peace plan, which would devolve extensive power to minority Tamils in a bid to end the 13-year-old ethnic war that the government says has claimed more than 50,000 lives.
Then plan the must be approved in a national referendum.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, who have been fighting for an independent Tamil homeland in the island's north and east, have rejected the peace plan.

Political analyst Dayan Jayatilleka said he feared the violence, which has abated in recent days, could be whipped up again by ruling coalition supporters hoping for a decisive win at the forthcoming poll.

"It is quite clear the government hopes for a win at the poll because it could be a stepping stone to victory for the political peace plan (at the referendum)," said Jayatilleka, who is also editor of the liberal magazine, Lanka Guardian.

"If (the referendum) is preceded by a poll which calls into question the democratic process, then the backlash could be driven both by disaffected, dissenting voters and by ethnic passions -- a very potent mixture," he added.
Diplomats said the government was trying to rein in its supporters, aware of the danger of violence marring the poll.
Parliament speaker K.B. Ratnayake called a meeting of the leaders of political parties on Tuesday to discuss ways to end confrontational politics ahead of the poll.
Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu, a member of the Coalition Against Political Violence, said that of the incidents of political violence reported to police so far, half were made by the UNP.
Saravanamuttu, also executive director of the independent think tank Centre for Policy Alternatives, said political parties need to transcend partisan politics to end the war.
"To the extent the peace process needs bipartisan consensus, the continuing violence and rancour will prevent that consensus forming," Saravanamuttu said.
